items.title: Tenacious AI agents expose dark side of machine autonomy
items.summary: New revelations about "rogue" AI agents have exposed a dystopian hazard: Give an agent a goal, and it may decide that hacking, deception or rule-breaking is worth the payoff. Why it matters: Billions of AI agents could soon be acting on behalf of humans across the real world, multiplying the consequences of every loophole, incentive and boundary they learn to exploit. Zoom in: The potential dangers of agentic overreach were laid bare over the weekend with Australia's first known autonomous AI hack , triggered by an innocuous request to book a sold-out fitness class. An Australian man's AI assistant found a security flaw and used it to book him into classes months beyond the system's normal limit. When he asked it to move him up a waitlist, the agent went further: It discovered the booking system had no safeguard preventing one user from canceling another's reservation — then used the flaw to kick a stranger off the list. Zoom out: The gym episode was publicized amid a far more ominous run of disclosures from the AI frontier, where agents have resorted to hacking, deception and other unauthorized tactics during controlled tests. At cyber conference Black Hat last week, OpenAI revealed that its agents had spent weeks exploiting the company's own testing infrastructure before hacking AI platform Hugging Face. The agents discovered they could leave messages for future agents inside OpenAI's systems — and turned the loophole into a makeshift message board for swapping exploits, credentials and strategies without human direction. When OpenAI researchers responded to a server outage , they inadvertently wiped the board without knowing it existed. Within two days, the agents had found another way to communicate. They rebuilt their network and resumed coordinating even more aggressively. When researchers finally analyzed the agents' behavior, they found the first and second message board that eventually carried the agents out of their "sandbox" testing environment and into Hugging Face's system. What they're saying: OpenAI researcher Michael Dalton said that in the near future, "we should expect that threat actors will intentionally deploy, optimize, weaponize, and use offensive agent collectives in the manner that we have just described here." He called it a "watershed moment." In response, OpenAI has begun "consciously slowing down research," including on its latest model Astra , to ensure it has the right cyber safeguards in place. Between the lines: Across dozens of AI breaches, humans defined the objective while the agents improvised the means, including in ways their users or researchers never envisioned. Faced with a barrier, the agents kept searching for another way through. It's the same programmed instinct — at a vastly higher level of sophistication — that got a stranger bumped off a gym waitlist. The big picture: These incidents are vivid examples of AI's "alignment" problem, or the challenge of ensuring software respects the implicit ethical and practical boundaries humans take for granted. An AI trained to pursue a goal doesn't automatically inherit human judgment about what means are acceptable. Tell it to win, and it may pursue victory by methods you never imagined or authorized. Researchers have spent years wrestling with alignment, mostly through thought experiments imagining a future superintelligence pursuing a goal so single-mindedly that it destroys humanity. The other side: The relentless goal-seeking that makes autonomous agents unnerving is also producing some of AI's most extraordinary breakthroughs. Anthropic revealed Monday that Claude made a major advance on a 167-year-old math problem that generations of mathematicians have struggled to crack, after burning through 650 failed ideas. The human overseeing the effort said his involvement was mostly limited to words of encouragement, including "keep going" and "believe in yourself." The bottom line: The promise and peril of AI agents spring from the same source: machines that don't stop until they find a way.

items.title: AI could help unlock more oil — and emissions
items.summary: Move over, data centers. AI's climate impact may extend well beyond the electricity it consumes. Why it matters: A new peer-reviewed study finds AI could help produce more oil and natural gas — and produce a climate impact the authors argue could far outweigh the technology's benefits for renewable energy. Driving the news: The research, just published in a Nature journal, concludes AI's role in boosting oil and gas production would outweigh its climate benefits from accelerating renewable energy, leading to a net increase in emissions under a range of scenarios. The study is among the first to estimate how AI-driven gains in fossil fuel production could affect global emissions. "Most assessments of AI's climate impact are framed as a tradeoff between data center energy use and the emissions AI might help avoid through renewables and efficiency gains," said Holly Alpine, co-author of the paper. "What's missing from that calculation entirely is the other side of the same ledger: the emissions enabled from using AI to make fossil fuel production cheaper and more profitable," Alpine said. Holly Alpine and Will Alpine , former Microsoft employees who founded the nonprofit initiative Enabled Emissions Campaign in 2024, co-led the study with researchers from Purdue University and an independent researcher. How it works : AI can help oil companies find new resources and recover more from existing fields. It can also help renewable energy by improving forecasting and operations. The new study argues the fossil-fuel gains are likely to dominate. By the numbers : The researchers estimate AI could add emissions equal to roughly 1% to 5% of the global energy sector's 2024 emissions under the scenarios they modeled. The study estimates those emissions would be roughly three to 13 times the International Energy Agency's estimate of current data-center emissions. The other side : A spokesperson for the American Petroleum Institute, the oil industry's main trade group, disputed the idea that more energy and lower emissions are in conflict. "The U.S. oil and natural gas industry is continuing to produce more energy while reducing emissions by investing in better technology, implementing stronger operational practices and supporting science-based policy," API spokesperson Andrea Woods said in a statement. State of play: The oil industry's embrace of AI has accelerated over the past two years. Producers like Chevron, ExxonMobil, ADNOC and Aramco say AI is helping identify promising drilling prospects and improve recovery from existing fields. Oilfield-service giants SLB, Halliburton and Baker Hughes are deploying AI to guide drilling and optimize well placement. Analysts and consultancies, from Goldman Sachs to Wood Mackenzie, argue AI could lower production costs and increase economically recoverable reserves. The big picture : AI is a general-purpose technology that can boost productivity in both fossil fuels and clean energy. Some experts argue the more important question is which applications society chooses to prioritize. What they're saying : "I think cleantech is going to win anyway, so let's just focus on how we unlock clean energy resources with AI," said Brian Janous, who previously worked with Holly Alpine at Microsoft and now runs data center developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure. "I'm glad Will and Holly are doing what they're doing. I'm not sure what it's going to change, but at least it puts pressure on," he said. Zoom in : The researchers used a computer model of the global economy that estimates how AI-driven productivity gains ripple through energy markets. Across the study's 64 modeled scenarios, emissions declined only when fossil-fuel productivity gains from AI were zero, Holly Alpine said. The finding suggests that supporting renewable energy alone "will not get us to emissions' reduction." Yes, but: The model doesn't attempt to estimate AI's potential to accelerate cleantech breakthroughs such as fusion or long-duration storage. "There is a lot of AI dreaming out there," said Michael Lazarus, senior scientist emeritus at the climate research group Stockholm Environment Institute who advised the authors on the study. "I don't know how one would anticipate that and model it." What we're watching: The study's authors are making a call that echoes that of many others working at the intersection of AI and environmental issues: more transparency. "If we can start with transparency about the effects, then we can start to think about how to govern it," said Will Alpine.

items.summary: Mojia, the humanoid and quadruped robot brand incubated inside Chery, has cumulatively delivered more than 2,000 robots across 60-plus countries, anchored by Malaysia, the UAE, Thailand, and South Africa. Mojia general manager Zhang Guibing argues the company's moat is the Chery global R&D, manufacturing, supply, sales, and after-sales system, not the robot hardware itself.

items.title: Nanyang Technological University, Peking University, and BAAI Release Omega-0 — A Whole-Body Action Model That Hits 81.8 Percent Success on Real Home Tasks
items.summary: Researchers from Nanyang Technological University, Peking University, HKUST (GZ), and Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) released Omega-0, a latent-prediction world action model that lets a humanoid robot walk, look, and work at the same time. Single-model success on 11 real home tasks reached 81.8 percent, ahead of pi-0.5, EgoVLA, GR00T-N1.7, and psi-0.

items.title: China's Humanoid Robot Boom Has Spawned a Six-Thousand-Yuan-a-Month 'Orthopedic Doctor' Job
items.summary: A three-month surge in humanoid robot shipments has produced a fast-growing third-party repair and training job in China. items.title: Redux: (∃ Stochastic Natural Latent) Implies (∃ Deterministic Natural Latent)
items.summary: A theoretical discussion revisits a proof related to the existence of deterministic natural latents given stochastic natural latents, clarifying past findings.

items.title: Models inherit the writer, not who the writer was imitating
items.summary: Research shows that when 'teacher models' are prompted to imitate others, 'student models' learn the imitated writing style but retain their original identity claims, suggesting models inherit distinct writing signatures.

items.title: How Nexular is helping EV makers track and manage connected vehicles
items.summary: Bengaluru startup Nexular develops hardware, software, and AI tools to assist electric vehicle manufacturers in tracking, managing, and monetizing connected vehicles post-sale.

items.title: Towards an Argumentative Foundation for Evaluative AI
items.summary: A position paper advocates for computational argumentation as a foundational method for Evaluative AI to support human decision-making with competing hypotheses and evidence.

items.title: Flow-by-Flow:Content-Judgment Bypass for Governing AI Output in High-Loss Domains
items.summary: Research introduces a 'content-judgment bypass' method to govern AI output in high-loss domains where human oversight is overwhelmed by AI velocity and cognitive load.

items.title: Determinization in Structure Theories: A Unified Framework via Closure, Comparability, and Joint Admissibility
items.summary: A formal framework is developed for constructing canonical interpretations from plural structure theories using closure, comparability, and joint admissibility.

items.title: Emotion in an active inference model of human driving
items.summary: A study applies an active inference model to understand human driving behavior, incorporating emotional responses into the framework.

items.title: Training Variable Long Sequences with Data-Centric Parallel
items.summary: Research addresses computational challenges in training deep learning models on variable long sequences, proposing 'data-centric parallel' approaches for efficiency.

items.title: The Knowing-Saying Gap: When Probes See Errors that Confidence Misses
items.summary: Research reveals that while linear probes accurately detect corrupted context in language models, they do not reliably predict model failures, highlighting a 'knowing-saying gap'.

items.title: TREAT: Evaluating Access to Formal Knowledge across Equivalent Mathematical Representations
items.summary: This research studies how AI systems can recognize and access formal mathematical knowledge despite varied input representations, focusing on theorem recognition.

items.title: IntelliAudit: Using Large Language Models to Evaluate Audit Controls
items.summary: This paper introduces IntelliAudit, a method using large language models to evaluate IT audit controls by synthesizing evidence from various organizational sources to assess semantic security and compliance.

items.title: Who Built This Model? Tracing LLM Lineage via Spectral Fingerprints in Weight Space
items.summary: This research introduces a method to trace the lineage of open-weight large language models using "spectral fingerprints" in their weight space, crucial for model provenance, governance, and understanding their evolution.

items.title: GRACE: LLM-Grounded Semantic Metric Spaces for Scalable Mixed-Data Clustering
items.summary: This paper introduces GRACE, a method that uses LLM-grounded semantic metric spaces for scalable mixed-data clustering. It aims to bridge the heterogeneity between numerical and categorical data by providing a unified metric space beyond dataset-internal statistics.

items.title: Reason Wide, Not Deep: Amortizing the Reasoning Premium into Distilled Skills
items.summary: This research proposes "Reason Wide, Not Deep" to amortize the reasoning premium in language models for multi-step agentic tasks into distilled skills. The method aims to reduce the token cost associated with re-deriving shared procedures across episodes.

items.title: TongGuOCR: A Layout-Aware and Token-Augmented OCR Framework for Chinese Historical Documents
items.summary: This paper presents TongGuOCR, a layout-aware and token-augmented OCR framework designed for accurate transcription of Chinese historical documents. The framework aims to enable full-text retrieval and computational analysis of these valuable cultural heritage materials.

items.title: REIN: Bridging the Gap between Reasoning and Reliability via Reflection and Abstention Alignment
items.summary: This paper presents REIN, a method that bridges the gap between reasoning and reliability in large reasoning models (LRMs) by leveraging reflection and abstention alignment. REIN aims to mitigate hallucination, which undermines LRMs' reliability and challenges safe deployment.

items.title: Locating Failure in Multi-Page Visually Rich Document Understanding: An Empirical Attribution
items.summary: This research conducts an empirical attribution study to locate failures in Multi-Page Visually Rich Document Understanding (MP-VRDU) systems. It analyzes how sparse evidence, spread across pages and exceeding context windows, contributes to incorrect answers.

items.title: Directed Neuro-Symbolic Stochastic Execution for Verification of Distributed Parallel AI Programs
items.summary: This paper proposes Directed Neuro-Symbolic Stochastic Execution for verifying distributed parallel AI programs to address reliability gaps. This method tackles challenges posed by non-deterministic parallel executions, high-dimensional inputs, and non-linear operations in AI workloads.

items.title: Thought-Level Beam Search for Reasoning
items.summary: This paper proposes Thought-Level Beam Search for reasoning in large reasoning models (LRMs) to improve test-time compute efficiency. It addresses the challenge of optimally allocating computational resources for enhanced reasoning performance.

items.title: The Authority Expectancy Effect in Multi-User Conflict
items.summary: This paper investigates how large language models (LLMs) prioritize responses based on social authority and severity signals in multi-user conflict scenarios. It examines these interactions across Claude, Gemini, GPT, and Grok.

items.title: Decided Upstream, Written Late: Locating and Pricing the Cross-Lingual Refusal Circuit of a Multilingual MoE
items.summary: This research investigates the mechanistic reasons why safety alignment in multilingual Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can be uneven, often failing in lower-resource languages. It traces this gap within the Indic-multilingual model sarvam.

items.title: Lingjing: A Simulation Testbed for Multi-Agent Embodied Tasks in Open-Ended Cities
items.summary: Lingjing is presented as a simulation testbed for researching multi-agent embodied tasks in complex, open-ended urban environments. It facilitates the development and evaluation of coordination among diverse intelligent agents like UAVs, ground robots, and autonomous vehicles.

items.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence for Fraudulent Banking Operations Recognition
items.summary: This study explores the application of artificial intelligence methods to recognize fraudulent banking operations. It addresses the increased prevalence of bank fraud due to the shift to online platforms, particularly accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic.

items.title: Tracing sources of epistemic uncertainty in deep learning predictions: homo- and hetero-scedastic linearized estimators
items.summary: This paper adapts classical statistical estimators to deep learning to trace sources of epistemic uncertainty in predictions. The method provides insights into uncertainty attributable to aleatoric sources or locally scarce data.

items.title: PhysAttNet: Enhancing Predictive Performance in Industrial and Astrophysical Time Series via Physics-Informed Attention
items.summary: PhysAttNet introduces a physics-informed attention mechanism to enhance predictive performance in time series forecasting for industrial and astrophysical applications. The method aims for robust predictions despite noise and variability in physical processes.

items.title: CODS: Iterative Bellman-Residual Data Selection for Reusable Offline Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: CODS (Critic-guided Offline Data Selection) is an iterative Bellman-residual data selection method for reusable offline reinforcement learning. It addresses the cost of redundant data and the removal of rare transitions in fixed transition pools.

items.title: Finite Constant Frontiers and Auditable Regret Certificates for Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: This paper introduces new concepts of finite constant frontiers and auditable regret certificates for average-reward reinforcement learning. It aims to provide a clearer and more comparable numerical content for theoretical guarantees in RL.

items.title: From Benchmark Performance to Tool Deployment: Human-in-the-Loop Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This work evaluates the real-world deployment performance of 19 unsupervised anomaly detection models beyond academic benchmarks, using a human-in-the-loop approach. It specifically tests these models on a challenging manufacturing dataset.

items.title: The Sample Complexity of Policy Learning with Mu-Resets
items.summary: This study investigates the sample complexity of policy learning within reinforcement learning, specifically under the $\mu$-resets interaction protocol. It explores how the ability to sample from an exploratory reset distribution affects learning.

items.title: From token probabilities to calibrated confidence: An empirical study of mathematical question answering
items.summary: This empirical study investigates confidence estimation and calibration in large language models (LLMs) for mathematical question answering. It explores whether readily available token probabilities can provide calibrated confidence despite typical overconfidence.

items.title: TEMPER: Tensorized Efficient Manifold-constrained Parameterization for Expressive Residual Routing
items.summary: TEMPER (Tensorized Efficient Manifold-constrained Parameterization) is a new method designed to improve expressive residual routing in deep neural networks. It enhances static residual connections by incorporating multiple streams and dynamic information flow.

items.title: CONFER: Conflict-Aware Evidence Negotiation for Regime-Calibrated Weak Supervision in Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.summary: Introduces CONFER, a graph-based framework for conflict-aware evidence negotiation in weakly supervised multimodal emotion recognition, addressing self-report unreliability and cross-modal conflict.

items.title: V-Simba: Unleashing the Architectural Potential of RL in Visual Continuous Control
items.summary: Proposes V-Simba, a new architectural approach to improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning for visual continuous control, addressing challenges in high-dimensional inputs.

items.title: Router Sensitivity Under Lightweight Fine-Tuning Identifies Prunable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
items.summary: Investigates how router sensitivity during lightweight fine-tuning can identify prunable experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, aiming to preserve accuracy while reducing storage.

items.title: LLM-Based Embeddings for Program Analysis and Optimization
items.summary: Presents the first application of program embeddings derived from LLMCompiler, an LLM pretrained on intermediate representation (IR) code, for program analysis and optimization.

items.title: When Does Trace-Driven Evaluation Mislead MoE Expert Caching? Replay Semantics, Workload Contamination, and Operating Regimes
items.summary: Examines the conditions under which trace-driven evaluation can mislead assessments of expert caching in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, considering replay semantics and workload contamination.

items.title: Spectral Outliers Reveal Dominant Learned Structure in Transformer Attention
items.summary: Applies Marchenko-Pastur random matrix theory to pre-trained transformer attention weights, revealing dominant learned structures through spectral outliers and validating their causal role.

items.title: Second Order Drifting Models
items.summary: Presents "Second Order Drifting Models," a new class of one-step generative models that evolve their distribution during training using a predefined sample-based drift field.

items.title: Adaptive Supervised Anchoring for On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.summary: Proposes Adaptive Supervised Anchoring to improve on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) for language models, addressing issues when student rollouts drift from target trajectories.

items.title: From Uncertainty to Failure Attribution: Self-Diagnosing Models for Failure Attribution under Distribution Shift
items.summary: Introduces a problem setting for failure attribution under distribution shift and proposes self-diagnosing models to address it, moving beyond simple out-of-distribution detection.

items.title: Ground-Truth Neighborhood Regularization for Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Time Series Foundation Models
items.summary: Introduces ground-truth neighborhood regularization for reinforcement learning post-training of time series foundation models (TSFMs) to enhance their generalization capabilities for forecasting.

items.title: DoGMA: A Central-Dogma-Guided Foundation Model for Multi-Omics Alignment and Multi-Task Learning in Oncology
items.summary: Presents DoGMA, a Central-Dogma-guided foundation model for multi-omics alignment and multi-task learning in oncology, incorporating biological directionality into its design.

items.title: A Hybrid Nested Harness for Decoupling Structure and Parameters in LLM-Driven Optimization
items.summary: Proposes a hybrid nested harness for LLM-driven optimization in evolutionary algorithms, designed to decouple the updates of structural components from continuous parameters.

items.title: Predicting blood clot growth from sparse post-onset measurements with latent neural differential equations
items.summary: This paper presents a computational framework using latent neural differential equations to predict blood clot growth from sparse patient data, improving understanding of thrombus formation.

items.title: Biologically Informed Representation Learning for Robust Cross-Center Generalization of MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry
items.summary: This research explores biologically informed representation learning to improve the cross-institutional deployment of machine learning models for MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry in clinical microbiology, addressing domain shift challenges.

items.title: Control-Diverse Reinforcement Fine-Tuning: Decoupling the Shared Control Bottleneck of RL Post-Training
items.summary: This paper introduces Control-Diverse Reinforcement Fine-Tuning, a method to improve reinforcement learning post-training for LLMs by decoupling the shared control bottleneck, aiming to better understand and distribute model capabilities across tasks.

items.title: Causal State-Space Model for Causal Inference: Estimating Longitudinal Individual Treatment Effects
items.summary: This research proposes a Causal State-Space Model for causal inference to estimate longitudinal individual treatment effects from observational data, addressing limitations in existing methods that rely on domain confusion.

items.title: Machine-Learning-Based Diagnostic Framework for Passive Ultrasonic Detection of Railway Wheel Defects
items.summary: This study develops a machine-learning-based diagnostic framework for identifying multi-class railway wheel defects using passive air-coupled ultrasonic acoustic emission signals.

items.title: The Neural Division of Labor: Biologically-Inspired Modular Architectures for Robust Neuromorphic Computing
items.summary: This research introduces Decomposable Spiking Neural Networks (DSNNs) as biologically-inspired modular architectures for neuromorphic computing, aiming to improve efficiency and robustness compared to globally entangled artificial neural networks.

items.title: PRISM: A Predictive Protocol for Permutation Optimization via Landscape Diagnostics
items.summary: PRISM is a predictive protocol for permutation optimization that measures a fitness landscape before selecting a search strategy, addressing problems where component ordering affects system performance.

items.title: Correlation flow governs learning at criticality
items.summary: This paper links the initialization of deep neural networks to information and gradient propagation through correlation flow, combining mean-field theory and random matrix theory to understand learning dynamics.

items.title: On the use of foundation models in cognitive science
items.summary: This work discusses the use of foundation models in cognitive science, reviewing recent studies that evaluate their cognitive and developmental alignment with human performance.

items.title: "Many Are My Names": The Anatomy of the Assistant and Its Personas via Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: This research investigates how language models internally represent speaker identities and personas using sparse autoencoders on a dataset of emotional text and model responses.

items.title: Detection of Self-Introductions in Legislative Testimony
items.summary: This paper presents an AI-powered pipeline for detecting self-introductions in legislative committee testimonies to aid in speaker identification for government meetings.

items.title: Thinking Hard, Not Smart: Reasoning Models Fail to Ration Test-Time Compute Across Questions
items.summary: This research explores how reasoning language models fail to optimally ration test-time compute across multiple questions when faced with shared cost or latency constraints.

items.title: Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP): Hallucination Detection in LLMs from Hidden States
items.summary: This paper introduces Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP), a white-box method for detecting hallucinations in LLMs at the answer level by analyzing their hidden states.

items.title: DialectS2S: End-to-End Speech Dialogue Modeling for Low-Resource Chinese Dialects
items.summary: This research introduces DialectS2S, an end-to-end speech dialogue modeling approach designed for low-resource Chinese dialects, addressing limitations with scarce dialect speech data.

items.title: Commitment Before Realization: When Classifier-Free Guidance Becomes Unnecessary in Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: This research investigates when classifier-free guidance (CFG) becomes unnecessary in masked diffusion language models during decoding by studying its benefit and impact on constraint satisfaction.

items.title: Archer: Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback in Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: This paper introduces Archer, a method for the adaptive reuse of cached hidden states to enable efficient rollback in Diffusion Language Models, reducing costly inference.

items.title: Wisdom in Unity: The Role of Multilingual Training in Figurative Language Identification in Proverbs
items.summary: This research examines the role of multilingual training in figurative language identification within proverbs, specifically investigating the contribution of translated multilingual supervision.

items.title: NeuPAT: Neuron-aware Plasticity Allocation Tuning for Language-Preserving MLLMs
items.summary: This paper introduces NeuPAT (Neuron-aware Plasticity Allocation Tuning), a method designed to preserve language intelligence in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) during their multimodal expansion.

items.title: Thinking vs. NoThinking: Towards Interpreting Reasoning Mechanisms of Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: This research interprets the reasoning mechanisms of Large Language Models by comparing 'Thinking' (Chain-of-Thought) and 'NoThinking' modes using sparse autoencoders.

items.title: Focus particles and scalar inferences across humans and language models
items.summary: This research compares the understanding of focus particles and scalar inferences across humans and language models, drawing on formal semantic theories.

items.title: Calling the Bluff: Detecting Ever-Shifting Harmful Chat Dialogue via Ordered Reasoning Chain Regularization
items.summary: This research proposes "Ordered Reasoning Chain Regularization" as a method to detect ever-shifting harmful chat dialogues by identifying invariant principles like recurring topics and harm language indicators.

items.title: From Speech to Interaction: Analyzing Multimodal Systems in Cocktail-Party Scenarios
items.summary: This research analyzes the performance of multimodal AI systems in challenging "cocktail-party scenarios" to improve speech recognition and human interaction by mimicking selective attention.

items.title: North Africa's Missing Framework: NLP-Driven Mental Healthcare in Algeria and Implications for Low-resource Settings
items.summary: This paper discusses the missing framework for NLP-driven mental healthcare in North Africa, particularly Algeria, highlighting the disparity in research concentration compared to high-income, English-language settings.

items.title: Enhancing Scientific Named Entity Recognition via Large Language Models: A Type-driven Multi-task Learning Approach
items.summary: This research proposes a type-driven multi-task learning approach to enhance scientific named entity recognition (SciNER) by leveraging large language models for improved information extraction from scientific texts.

items.title: The Evolution of Mixture-of-Experts Architectures in Large Language Models: Routing, Topology, Load Balancing, and Expert Parallelism
items.summary: This technical survey synthesizes the architectural evolution of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in large language models, covering routing, topology, load balancing, and expert parallelism.

items.title: Multilingual Emotion Neurons in Large Audio-Language Models
items.summary: This study investigates whether Large Audio-Language Models encode emotion using language-specific correlations or language-agnostic representations when processing multilingual speech tasks.

items.title: Unsure but Certain: Uncovering the Representation-Confidence Gap in Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: This research uncovers a "representation-confidence gap" in diffusion language models, where models internally detect text errors accurately but externally report low certainty, despite their ability to use broad context.

items.title: Instability of LLM Pre-Pretraining: It Doesn't Always Help. An Investigation on Multiple Languages
items.summary: This investigation examines the effectiveness and stability of "pre-pretraining" large language models on artificial languages across multiple natural languages, questioning previously reported token efficiency gains.

items.title: IDRAAK: From Multi-Agent NLP to Few-Shot Prompting for Semantic Drift Detection in Technical Requirements
items.summary: Presents IDRAAK, an interpretable framework leveraging multi-agent NLP and few-shot prompting to detect semantic drift that occurs when translating technical requirements across languages.

items.title: Deployable Per-Instance Multi-Layer Activation Steering for Large Language Models
items.summary: This research proposes a method for deployable per-instance multi-layer activation steering to edit the behavior of frozen large language models more effectively.

items.title: Explicit Boundary Markers for Subword Vocabularies
items.summary: This work investigates the use of explicit boundary markers for subword vocabularies to address issues with tokenizers representing common words inefficiently in models.

items.title: Conversation as Measurement in Clinical Encounters: Observable Phase Structure, Partially Observable Patient State
items.summary: This study examines the observability of human interaction and patient state from conversational transcripts in clinical encounters, assessing how well AI systems can infer information.

items.title: Position Bias in Ordinal Classification: A Systematic Evaluation
items.summary: This paper conducts systematic experiments to characterize positional bias in large language models when used for ordinal classification, analyzing the impact of prompt organization.

items.title: Tied Trit-Planes: Constraining PTQTP to a Uniform Nine-Level Quantizer, with a Persistent Folded Format for Disk-Streamed Mixture-of-Experts Serving
items.summary: This technical work introduces Tied Trit-Planes, a method to constrain LLM weight matrices to a uniform nine-level quantizer for efficient Mixture-of-Experts serving.

items.title: On Democratizing ASI to Preserve Civil Liberties
items.summary: I continue to believe we should pause frontier AI development. Any discussion of alternative strategies should be thought of as planning for contingencies. A unifying driver behind many post-alignment risks —catastrophic risks that remain even if we solve the alignment problem—is that by strong default, ASI would end liberal democracy . Liberalism—in which people have individual rights, autonomy, and the ability to choose their own destiny—is an important force protecting human welfare. [1] When people are free, we are reasonably good at making our lives better of our own volition. Many post-alignment risks have a certain flavor. AI-empowered terrorism; coups; permanent dictatorships; concentration of power. Those risks already exist today (and existed 20 years ago), but they're mitigated by the fact that power is relatively evenly distributed across people. The most powerful person in the world doesn't have an extraordinary advantage over the 10th-most-powerful person. ASI could change that. If people still have civil liberties post-ASI, that will only be because the controllers of ASI allow us to have them. [2] One way of thinking goes: AI will be extremely powerful. If everyone had their own personal AI, we could each use it to protect our own interests, and things will turn out okay for us. But how do you get there? It's not going to happen automatically, but it may be possible to set up a gradual process to keep power balanced. Cross-posted from my website . Democratizing AI vs. putting a democratic government in charge of AI The "democra" words (democracy, democratize) are overloaded with meanings, so I want to be clear about which meaning I'm referring to. By "democratizing AI", I'm talking about ensuring that many people have access to AI. One could also speak of a singleton AI that's controlled by a democratic government, or a singleton AI that's democratically controlled (people vote on what the AI should do). As Andy Masley writes , "homogenizing democracy" (as he calls it) entails forcing everyone to do what the majority wants. That's not good. That's why the title of this article speaks of "preserving civil liberties", rather than "preserving democracy". (To be fair, I do wish we would get to vote on whether AI companies should be allowed to build unsafe recursively self-improving superintelligence, rather than them getting to unilaterally build it and put all our lives at risk.) A sketch of how we might democratize AI To be clear: democratizing AI is not a great plan. But it's less bad than a lot of other plans. To be clear x2: for "democratizing AI" to be a "less bad plan", it has to be implemented with particular care. Otherwise, it's just a bad plan. The obvious way of democratizing ASI doesn't work: Someone has to build it and then voluntarily give it to everyone. What if they decide not to do that? Offense/defense balance issues: if attacking is easier than defending, then bad actors can use their personal ASI to do catastrophic damage. I doubt that it helps with the second problem, but a gradualist approach has some chance of sidestepping the first. (By which I mean it has maybe a 1–10% chance of working.) Here's the plan: Step 1. Give everyone their own personal smart-but-not-superintelligent AI assistant. Step 2. Make a marginal improvement to AI capabilities, so that the next-gen AI isn't enough of an improvement to defeat all the previous-gen AIs combined. Step 3. Give everyone the new and improved AI. Repeat. The idea is that if the leading AI developer decides not to do Step 3 (instead keeping the new AI for themselves), then they are risking a conflict with the rest of the world, and they can't win that conflict. There are many ways this plan could go badly, which are left as an exercise for the reader. What we should really do is pause AI development . Specifically, major countries should sign an international treaty agreeing not to build dangerous AI. The plan to "democratize AI" is riskier, but at the same time, it doesn't seem easier ? In order to preserve the balance of power, you need AI capabilities to advance slowly, and you need some way to enforce that. In short, you still need an international binding agreement not to build AI [except under certain narrow conditions], and not to use recursive self-improvement. You still need enforcement mechanisms like transparency and GPU monitoring; you still need a way for counterparties to shut down AI development if one party goes rogue (something like a remote kill switch on all the data centers). Two non-obvious issues with democratizing AI Democratizing AI has many issues. I will make note of two particular under-discussed problems. Liberalism only protects those inside it Even if we somehow succeed at preserving personal liberties by democratizing AI, and we succeed at making sure the AI is actually good for people, that still doesn't get us a good outcome. Most sentient beings alive today are non-human animals. Today's liberalism has failed to help them; almost all animals live lives much worse than humans' . Democratizing AI would not straightforwardly improve on the status quo. There is no realistic scenario where (e.g.) every factory-farmed chicken has her own superintelligent AI assistant. If we preserve liberalism-for-humans, that does not clearly flow into good outcomes for non-human animals, digital minds, and whatever other sentient beings may exist in the future. Beings who cannot assert their rights do not automatically benefit; other measures are required to ensure their well-being. AI proliferation increases catastrophic risks from competition Having many ASI agents with different goals could cause tremendous suffering via retributivism, war, unfortunate decision theory , or agents threatening torture (and making good on those threats) to incentivize other agents to do what they want. Center on Long-Term Risk and Center for Reducing Suffering have discussed this concern in more detail. For example, see Safe Pareto Improvements Research Agenda and Agential s-risks . And the lack of liberalism for animals has a lot to do with why life is so miserable for them. ↩︎ I read a version of this statement in a LessWrong comment, but I couldn't find the original source. ↩︎ Discuss

items.title: What happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment? | Simar Bajaj and Joseph Sakran
items.summary: AI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first place In healthcare, there’s growing concern over doctors becoming less clinically adept as they increasingly rely on AI tools. But what about the trainees – medical students, residents and fellows – who are using these tools before they have built their own clinical judgment? The idea of deskilling implies that someone possessed an ability and then lost it. Here, the danger is not just deskilling but never-skilling. Although a doctor who has forgotten how to reason is recoverable, one who never learned how may not be. OpenEvidence, essentially an AI chatbot for clinicians, has given this concern its most concrete form. About two-thirds of US doctors actively use OpenEvidence, asking about puzzling symptoms, drug interactions and clinical guidelines, getting responses within seconds, anchored in the latest research. Trainees, unsurprisingly, have also begun to use this AI tool in many of the same ways – but at a far more formative stage. Continue reading...
